title: Nine Instructional Moves for Teaching Texts
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: This concise article by Stuart argues that every text-based lesson — regardless of subject or grade level — requires only nine instructional moves, grouped around three phases of the reading experience: before, during, and after. Stuart contends that teachers consistently over-complicate text-based instruction, but that the goal is always the same: help students understand a text, then do something with that understanding. The nine moves include pre-reading strategies (hook, vocabulary preview, purpose-setting), during-reading strategies (modeling, guided practice, independent grappling), and post-reading moves (discussion, debate, writing). Stuart notes that his students show no sign of revolt when he uses these same nine pieces all year with dozens of different texts — suggesting that variety in content, not variety in method, is what keeps engagement alive. The article frames mastery of these nine moves as a professional investment in students' long-term good, since they develop transferable skills for wrestling with complex texts across disciplines.
points: Every text-based lesson has two objectives: help students understand the text, then do something with that understanding — all nine moves serve one of these two aims
Teachers over-complicate text instruction; limiting the repertoire to nine well-practiced moves allows students to internalize a predictable, confidence-building structure
Pre-reading moves (hook, vocabulary preview, purpose-setting) prime students to read productively by connecting to prior knowledge and establishing a clear reading goal
Post-reading moves — discussion, debate, writing — develop the transferable academic skills (analyze, argue, compare, summarize) that define college and career readiness
Repeating the same nine moves with diverse texts all year maintains engagement through the richness of content, not the novelty of method — a durable instructional philosophy
